profile.campus: Lebanon, Warren County, Ohio (CyrusOne CIN5 campus)
profile.reading:
Per CyrusOne's own facility page, CIN5 sits at 401 Kingsview Drive, Lebanon, OH 45036 on a 123-acre site, publishing 400,000 sq ft of technical IT space and 12 MW of total IT capacity, with a 24x7x365 staffed network operations control center and ISO 27001/SOC 2 Type II certification.

This facility is part of CyrusOne's Cincinnati-metro cluster, the company's home market: Wikipedia's CyrusOne entry states Cincinnati Bell purchased a stake in CyrusOne for $525 million in 2010 and divested it in 2015 after CyrusOne's 2013 IPO; the company was originally founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) acquired it for approximately $15 billion. The Cincinnati cluster spans buildings in Cincinnati proper, Lebanon, and Butler and Warren Counties in Ohio, plus a related facility across the Ohio River in Florence, Kentucky, reflecting the metro's historical role as CyrusOne's founding market before the company's national and international expansion.

Ohio's Cincinnati metro sits within the PJM Interconnection regional transmission grid, and Duke Energy is the dominant electric utility serving the Cincinnati area; PJM has separately flagged rising data center electricity demand across its multi-state footprint (which spans much of the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, including Northern Virginia's much larger concentration of facilities) as a factor in its long-term capacity planning. Cincinnati's relatively central US location, moderate climate, and status as CyrusOne's founding home market, rather than proximity to any single hyperscale anchor tenant, are what have kept the company concentrating multiple buildings in this metro even as its larger growth in recent years has shifted toward Texas, Virginia, and international markets.

reading.body:
Ohio's largest published data center holds 12 MW of IT capacity, enough for roughly 300 AI training racks, but most of the state's 76 facilities disclose no power figures at all.

CyrusOne Lebanon sits in the Cincinnati metro region as part of a larger cluster spanning multiple counties. The 12 MW facility occupies 400,000 square feet and ranks first among Ohio's eight data centers with published capacity. This transparency is rare. The remaining 68 mapped facilities in Ohio publish nothing about their power draw, making it impossible to assess whether the state's total AI infrastructure is constrained by electrical supply, building availability, or something else entirely.

The facility's certifications indicate it was built for regulated enterprise workloads, not optimized for AI training. SOC 2, HIPAA, FISMA, and ISO 27001 compliance suggest readiness for healthcare, finance, and government compute. Green Globes environmental certification is included. None of these credentials reveal whether the building or its power supply can support the density or duration that large-scale AI training requires.

CyrusOne was taken private in 2022 by KKR and Global Infrastructure Partners for 15 billion dollars. Private ownership typically correlates with opacity. No campus-wide power figure is published, and individual building loads within the cluster remain undisclosed. Without visibility into Ohio's full installed capacity or utilization rates, the state's role in AI infrastructure scaling cannot be measured.
